text:
===== FILE 2584__1.pdf =====
August 10, 2025 
 
Department of Veterans Affairs 
810 Vermont Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20420 
 
Re: Docket No. VA-2025-VHA-0073 / RIN 2900-AS31 
Proposed Rule: Exclusion of Abortion and Abortion Counseling from VA Medical 
Benefits 
 
Dear Secretary Collins: 
I am writing to express my serious concerns about the VA's proposal to eliminate abortion 
coverage from the medical benefits package for veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries. After 
reviewing the proposed rule and its supporting materials, I believe this reversal would be a 
mistake that ignores both data and the real needs of women who have served our country. 
The VA's justification relies heavily on the fact that fewer women used these services than 
initially projected, about 140 per year instead of the anticipated 1,000+ ("Exclusion of 
Abortion" 2). But this interpretation misses the point entirely. Low utilization doesn't 
necessarily mean low need. Has the VA considered that women might face significant barriers 
accessing these services? Geographic distance, provider availability, stigma, or simply not 
knowing the services exist could all explain these numbers. Without investigating these 
factors, the VA is making assumptions that could harm veterans. 
What's particularly troubling is that the VA hasn't provided any data about what happened to 
the 140 women who did receive care under the expanded policy. Were their lives improved? 
Were serious health complications prevented? Did they avoid financial hardship? These are 
the questions that matter when determining if a service is "needed." 
The medical community has extensively studied this issue. The landmark Turnaway Study, 
which followed nearly 1,000 women over ten years, found that women denied wanted 
abortions experienced higher rates of poverty, were more likely to stay with abusive 
partners, and showed increased anxiety compared to women who received abortion 
care (Foster et al. 956-957). Research consistently shows that women who can access 
comprehensive reproductive healthcare, including abortion services, have better 
physical health outcomes, greater economic stability, and improved mental health 
(Ralph et al. 78). The VA's proposal simply ignores this evidence without explanation. 

Women veterans aren't just statistics, they're individuals who've sacrificed for our country and 
often carry invisible wounds. One in three women veterans reports experiencing military 
sexual trauma (Kimerling et al. 2438). Many live in rural areas hours from the nearest civilian 
provider. Some have service-connected disabilities that make pregnancy particularly risky. 
These women have earned the right to comprehensive healthcare through their service, and 
they deserve better than to have their options limited based on political winds rather than 
medical necessity. 
The VA has built trust with veterans through trauma-informed care and understanding of 
military culture. For many women veterans, their VA provider is the only doctor they trust. 
Taking away services from these providers forces veterans into unfamiliar settings at 
vulnerable moments. 
What concerns me most is how this proposal determines what constitutes "needed" medical 
care. The statutory language hasn't changed since 1999, yet the VA's interpretation has flip-
flopped based solely on who occupies the White House. This isn't how evidence-based 
medicine should work. If the VA can reverse 23 years of policy, then change it again after just 
three years, what does this say about the stability and reliability of veteran healthcare? 
The proposal fails to account for the true costs of this policy change: emergency room visits 
when routine care is denied, mental health treatment for forced pregnancies, family instability, 
children growing up in poverty, and perhaps most importantly, the message it sends to women 
considering military service about how their country will treat them after they've served. 
Studies show that women denied abortions are four times more likely to live below the Federal 
Poverty Level and three times more likely to be unemployed than women who received 
abortion care (Foster 182-183). 
Instead of this abrupt reversal, I urge the VA to take a measured approach. First, study what 
actually happened during the past three years. Interview the women who used these services 
and those who needed but couldn't access them. Analyze the health outcomes, both physical 
and mental. Look at the financial impact on veteran families. 
Second, survey women veterans broadly about their healthcare needs and experiences. Don't 
assume, ask them directly what they need from their VA healthcare. 
Third, if changes must be made, ensure that clear exceptions remain for cases involving rape, 
incest, and threats to maternal health, not just life. The distinction between "life" and "health" 
may seem semantic in Washington, but it can mean everything to a woman facing a pregnancy 
complication. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists emphasizes that 
"pregnancy-related emergencies require immediate, evidence-based medical interventions" 

and that delays caused by restrictive policies can "jeopardize patient health and safety" 
(ACOG). 
The men and women who have worn our nation's uniform deserve healthcare decisions based 
on medical evidence and their actual needs, not political ideology. This proposal represents a 
step backward that will harm veterans who have already given so much. I strongly urge the 
VA to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the current policy while conducting the 
thoughtful, evidence-based analysis that such an important decision demands. 
Our veterans answered the call when our nation needed them. Now it's our turn to ensure 
they receive the comprehensive healthcare they've earned, all of it, without politically 
motivated exclusions. 
Thank you for your consideration of these comments and for your service to our nation's 
veterans. 
 
Respectfully, 
Ryan Heckman 
Veteran of the U.S. Air Force 2007-2011 
Alfred, NY 
 
Citations 
1. American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG). "Facts Are 
Important: Abortion Is Healthcare." ACOG Clinical, 2023, 
www.acog.org/advocacy/facts-are-important/abortion-is-healthcare. 
2. "Exclusion of Abortion and Abortion Counseling from Veterans Health 
Administration Medical Benefits Package and Civilian Health and Medical Program 
of the Department of Veterans Affairs." Federal Register, vol. 90, no. 147, 2 Aug. 2025, 
pp. 1-5. 
3. Foster, Diana Greene. The Turnaway Study: Ten Years, a Thousand Women, and the 
Consequences of Having—or Being Denied—an Abortion. Scribner, 2020. 
4. Foster, Diana Greene, et al. "Socioeconomic Outcomes of Women Who Receive 
and Women Who Are Denied Wanted Abortions in the United States." American 
Journal of Public Health, vol. 108, no. 3, 2018, pp. 956-959. 
5. Kimerling, Rachel, et al. "The Veterans Health Administration and Military Sexual 
Trauma." American Journal of Public Health, vol. 97, no. 12, 2007, pp. 2437-2442. 

6. Ralph, Lauren J., et al. "Self-reported Physical Health of Women Who Did and Did 
Not Terminate Pregnancy After Seeking Abortion Services: A Cohort Study." Annals 
of Internal Medicine, vol. 171, no. 2, 2019, pp. 75-83.
